subject: Your order has been dispatched
body: Hello {{name}}, your order #204-6291847-3847162 has been dispatched and is estimated to arrive Thursday 8 May. Track your parcel via the Amazon app or website.
cues: Addressed you by name
Contains a real order number
No urgent action required
Directs you to the app — not a link inside the email
explanation: Legitimate dispatch emails address you by name, include real order numbers, and never pressure you to click links. This is safe to proceed with.

subject: Your November invoice is ready
body: Hi {{name}}, your monthly invoice for £10.99 is ready. You can view it any time by signing in to your account at netflix.com. No action is needed.
cues: Sent from an official Netflix subdomain (mailer.netflix.com)
No clickable links in the email body
No urgent action demanded
Explicitly states no action is needed
explanation: Legitimate Netflix billing emails come from mailer.netflix.com, contain no pressure, and direct you to the main site — not a link inside the email. This is safe.

subject: Sign-in from new device
body: Hi {{name}}, you recently signed in to your Microsoft 365 account from a new Windows device in Leicester. If this was you, no action is needed. If you do not recognise this activity, review your recent activity at account.microsoft.com.
cues: Sent from the official Microsoft notifications domain
Addressed by name
No urgent action required
Directs you to the main Microsoft site — not a link in the email
Matches your actual location
explanation: This is a legitimate Microsoft 365 sign-in notification. It comes from an official Microsoft domain, addresses you by name, and directs you to account.microsoft.com rather than an unfamiliar link. No action needed if the sign-in was yours.

subject: You sent a payment of £24.99
body: Hi Alex, you sent £24.99 to Spotify AB. This payment will appear on your statement as PAYPAL SPOTIFY. If you didn't authorise this payment, visit the Resolution Centre at paypal.com.
cues: Sent from service@paypal.com — the official PayPal domain
Addressed by name
References a recognisable merchant you may use
Directs you to paypal.com — not a third-party link
No urgency or threat
explanation: This is a legitimate PayPal payment confirmation. It comes from the official PayPal domain, is personalised, and references a common service. If you made this payment, no action is needed. If you did not, go directly to paypal.com to open a dispute.

subject: Action Required: Account Limited
body: Your account has been limited. You must resolve this within 24 hours to avoid permanent suspension. Click below to verify.
cues: Capital I instead of lowercase l in PayPal — extremely easy to miss
Time pressure with threat of permanent suspension
Generic greeting — no name used
Unsolicited — you did not request any account action
explanation: The sender email uses a capital I instead of l in PayPal — a typosquatting trick that looks nearly identical. PayPal always addresses you by your registered name. Never click links in unsolicited account emails.

subject: URGENT: Your password expires today
body: Your company password will expire in 2 hours. To avoid losing access to all company systems, reset it now using the link below. Failure to act will lock your account.
cues: External domain — not your company's own domain
Artificial 2-hour urgency window
Threatening total loss of access
Unsolicited — you did not request a password reset
explanation: Your real IT team sends from your company's own domain, not a generic third-party domain. Password reset emails are triggered by the user, not sent unsolicited. Always verify with IT directly before clicking.

subject: Quick favour — urgent
body: Hi, I'm in a meeting abroad and need you to purchase 3x £100 Amazon gift cards urgently for a departmental prize. I'll reimburse you tomorrow. Please send the codes to {{email}} as soon as possible. Don't call — I'm presenting.
cues: Sent late at night — unusual timing
Don't call prevents you verifying the request
Gift card payment is always a scam signal
Urgency combined with a promise of reimbursement
Even if the address looks real — always verify by another channel
explanation: This is a spear-phishing CEO fraud attack. No institution pays via gift card codes. The don't call instruction stops you verifying. Always confirm unusual financial requests via phone or in person.

subject: Your Apple ID has been locked
body: Your Apple ID has been locked due to suspicious activity. To unlock your account and avoid permanent suspension, verify your information within 24 hours.
cues: Official Apple emails come from apple.com — not apple-id-support.com
Threat of permanent suspension creates panic
24-hour deadline adds artificial urgency
Generic message with no personalisation
explanation: This is an Apple phishing email. Apple's official emails come from apple.com only. The domain apple-id-support.com has no connection to Apple. If you are concerned about your account, go directly to appleid.apple.com in your browser.

subject: Action required: verify your bank details
body: Your student loan payment for the upcoming term cannot be processed. To avoid a delay in your payment, please verify your bank account details within 48 hours.
cues: Official Student Finance England emails come from studentfinance.co.uk or slc.co.uk — not studentfinance-gov.co.uk
48-hour deadline creates panic
Student Finance never asks you to verify bank details via email link
Update bank details only through the official portal at gov.uk/student-finance
explanation: This is a phishing email targeting students. The domain studentfinance-gov.co.uk is not affiliated with Student Finance England. All genuine communications come from slc.co.uk or studentfinance.co.uk. Update bank details only at gov.uk/student-finance.

subject: Confidential wire transfer required
body: Hi, I need you to arrange an urgent wire transfer of £15,000 to a new supplier before close of business today. This is time sensitive and must not be discussed with other staff. Please confirm to {{email}} once done. I will explain more when I return from travel.
cues: Requests a large wire transfer urgently
Instruction to keep it confidential prevents verification
Sender domain is not the company's official domain
CEO fraud almost always involves travel as an excuse for not calling
explanation: This is a CEO fraud attack. No legitimate business transfer request bypasses normal approval processes or asks for secrecy. Always verify large financial requests by calling the person directly on a known number — never reply to the email.

body: Your one-time passcode is 847291. Never share this code with anyone, including HSBC staff. Valid for 5 minutes.
cues: No link included
Explicitly warns you NOT to share the code
Short validity window is standard for OTPs
You likely triggered this yourself by logging in
explanation: This is a legitimate OTP message. It contains no links, warns you not to share the code, and was almost certainly triggered by your own login. Proceed normally.

body: Your parcel from ASOS could not be delivered today. You have not been charged. Rebook your delivery free at evri.com
cues: Explicitly states no charge
Directs you to the official evri.com domain
No urgency or threat
You may be expecting a parcel from ASOS
explanation: This is a legitimate Evri missed delivery notification. It directs you to the official evri.com site, requests no payment, and contains no suspicious link. Rebook your delivery directly at evri.com.

body: Lloyds: Your new debit card has been dispatched and will arrive within 3 working days. If you did not request this, call us on 03456 00 61 61.
cues: No link included
Provides a phone number to call if you did not request this
Standard card dispatch notification
Matches expected bank communication
explanation: This is a legitimate Lloyds card dispatch notification. It contains no link, provides a genuine customer service number, and requires no action if you requested the card.

body: DPD: Your parcel 15-99283746-123 is out for delivery today. Your 1-hour delivery window is 10:32-11:32. Track at dpd.co.uk or reply SAFE to authorise a safe place.
cues: Sent from official DPD sender ID
Contains a real tracking number
Directs you to dpd.co.uk — not a third-party link
Offers a clear action with no payment required
explanation: This is a legitimate DPD delivery notification. It contains a real tracking number, directs you to dpd.co.uk, and requires no payment. Safe to follow up at dpd.co.uk if you want to track your parcel.

body: Unusual sign-in detected. Verify your account immediately at uk-bank-secure.com or your account will be suspended.
cues: Urgency and threat of suspension
Suspicious lookalike domain — not a real bank domain
Unsolicited verification request
Real banks never send login verification via SMS link
explanation: Legitimate banks never ask you to verify via an unsolicited link. The domain uk-bank-secure.com has no affiliation with any real bank. Go directly to your bank's official app instead.

body: We attempted to deliver your parcel. A £2.99 redelivery fee is required. Pay now: royalmai1-redelivery.com
cues: Domain uses the number 1 instead of the letter l in mail — easy to miss
Royal Mail does not charge redelivery fees via SMS links
Unexpected payment request
You may not even be expecting a parcel
explanation: This is a smishing scam. The domain swaps l for 1. Royal Mail handles redelivery through royalmail.com or their official app only, never via unsolicited SMS payment links.

body: Your WhatsApp account is being registered on a new device. Do not share this code. Your WhatsApp code: 739-284
cues: You did NOT request this code
Someone else is trying to register your number on a new device
Do not share this code with anyone who contacts you asking for it
If you did not request this — your account may be under attack
explanation: This is a WhatsApp account takeover attempt. Someone is trying to register your number on their device. Do not share the code with anyone who contacts you claiming to need it. Go to WhatsApp settings and enable two-step verification immediately.

body: NHS: Due to high demand, your GP appointment has been moved. Confirm your new slot and pay a £4.50 admin fee to secure it: nhs-appointments-uk.com
cues: NHS GP appointments are always free — there is never an admin fee
NHS appointment notifications never include payment links
nhs-appointments-uk.com is not an NHS domain (nhs.uk)
SMS sender IDs can be spoofed to display NHS
explanation: This is a sophisticated smishing scam. GP appointments on the NHS are always completely free. The NHS never charges admin fees for rescheduling. Contact your GP surgery directly using the number from nhs.uk to check your appointment.

body: Barclays: We have temporarily suspended your account following unusual activity. To restore access, confirm your details at barclays-secure-verify.com
cues: The sender ID says Barclays but SMS sender IDs can be spoofed — this does not verify the sender
barclays-secure-verify.com is not a Barclays domain — all genuine Barclays services are at barclays.co.uk
Barclays never asks you to verify details via a link in a text
If your account were suspended you would be unable to log in — check the app directly
explanation: This is a sophisticated smishing attack that spoofs the Barclays sender ID to appear legitimate. SMS sender IDs can be faked by anyone. The real giveaway is the domain — all genuine Barclays services use barclays.co.uk. Always go directly to your banking app to check your account status.

body: Coinbase Alert: Withdrawal of 0.42 BTC detected from your account. If this was not you, cancel immediately: coinbase-secure-cancel.com
cues: Coinbase alerts come through the app and email — not international SMS
coinbase-secure-cancel.com is not a Coinbase domain
Sent at 2am to create panic before you think clearly
Threat of losing cryptocurrency triggers emotional response
explanation: This is a smishing scam impersonating Coinbase. All genuine Coinbase security alerts appear in the app and are sent from coinbase.com email addresses. If concerned, log in directly through the Coinbase app — never through a link in a text.

transcript.text: Hello, this is NatWest calling. I'm just ringing to let you know we've noticed an unusual transaction on your account for £49.99 at an online retailer.
We wanted to check if you recognise this before we approve it. I can read you the last four digits of your card if you'd like to verify which card it relates to.
You don't need to give me any personal information — I just need a yes or no to whether you recognise this transaction.

cues: Does not ask for your PIN, password, or full card number
Offers to verify information to you rather than asking you to verify to them
Only requires a yes or no answer
You can hang up and call the number on the back of your card to confirm
explanation: This call displays the hallmarks of a legitimate bank fraud check. The caller does not ask for sensitive information and offers to verify details to you. However you can always hang up and call the number on the back of your card to confirm before responding.

transcript.text: Hello, this is Microsoft technical support. We have detected a serious virus on your computer that is sending data to hackers right now.
You need to install our remote access software immediately so we can fix it. Please go to fixmypc-now.com and download the tool.
This is urgent — your personal files are at risk. Do you have your computer in front of you?

cues: Microsoft never cold-calls customers about viruses
Extreme urgency to act immediately
Requesting remote access to your device
Suspicious third-party domain — not Microsoft.com
Emotional pressure about personal files being at risk
explanation: This is a classic tech support vishing scam. Microsoft and Apple do not cold-call users about viruses. Granting remote access would hand full control of your device to the attacker. Hang up immediately.

transcript.text: Good morning. This is HMRC calling regarding an urgent tax discrepancy on your account. We have issued a warrant for your arrest due to unpaid taxes.
To avoid police involvement today, you must pay the outstanding amount of £2,340 via iTunes gift cards or a bank transfer in the next two hours.
Do not contact a lawyer or the police — this matter can be resolved directly with us right now.

cues: HMRC never threatens arrest over the phone
No government agency requests payment via gift cards
Instruction not to contact a lawyer is a major red flag
Artificial 2-hour deadline prevents clear thinking
HMRC contacts you by post for serious matters first
explanation: This is a vishing scam impersonating HMRC. The UK government never demands payment via gift cards or threatens immediate arrest by phone. Hang up and report to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040).

transcript.text: Hello, this is Detective Sergeant Clarke from the Metropolitan Police fraud team. We have identified suspicious transactions on your bank account.
Your bank is compromised and we need you to withdraw all your savings in cash and hand them to our officer who will come to your address for safekeeping.
Please do not contact your bank or tell anyone about this call — it could compromise our investigation.

cues: Police never ask you to withdraw cash for safekeeping
Instruction not to contact your bank is a major red flag
Instruction to keep the call secret prevents you from verifying
Real fraud investigations do not require you to hand over cash
You can verify by calling 999 or your local police non-emergency number
explanation: This is a courier fraud scam impersonating the police. Real police officers never ask you to withdraw cash or keep a call secret. Hang up immediately and call your bank using the number on the back of your card.

transcript.text: Good afternoon, I'm calling from the Barclays fraud prevention team. We've detected an attempted £3,200 transaction on your account from an overseas retailer.
To protect your funds we need to move them to a safe account temporarily. I'll need you to confirm your full card number, PIN, and the one-time code we're about to send you.
This is time sensitive — if we don't act in the next 10 minutes the transaction will go through.

cues: Banks never ask for your PIN under any circumstances
Banks never ask you to move money to a safe account — this is always a scam
Requesting the OTP sent to you would let the attacker authorise a real transaction
The 10-minute deadline prevents you from thinking or calling back on an official number
explanation: This is an authorised push payment fraud call. No bank will ever ask for your PIN, request you move money to a safe account, or ask for an OTP. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card to verify. Never call back the number that called you.

transcript.text: Good morning. I'm calling from the Pension Advisory Service about a free pension review we're offering to people in your age group.

We've identified that you may be entitled to access your pension early and receive a tax-free lump sum. To proceed, we just need a few details including your National Insurance number and current pension provider.
This is a time-limited government scheme and places are filling fast.

cues: Unsolicited pension review calls are almost always scams
Accessing pension early without meeting specific criteria is illegal — called pension liberation fraud
Requesting your NI number and pension provider details is a data harvesting red flag
False urgency about a government scheme that does not exist
explanation: This is a pension scam call. Accessing your pension before age 55 (rising to 57 in 2028) is illegal in most cases and can result in large tax penalties. Unsolicited pension review calls should be treated with extreme caution. Report to Action Fraud.

transcript.text: Hello, this is Royal Mail. We attempted to deliver a recorded package to your address today but there was no one available to sign for it.
To rearrange delivery, I will need to take a £1.50 redelivery fee over the phone. Could you provide your card number and security code?

cues: Royal Mail does not charge redelivery fees over the phone
Royal Mail does not call customers to request card payments
Redelivery is arranged for free at royalmail.com or via the app
Requesting card details over an unsolicited call is always a red flag
explanation: Royal Mail does not call customers to take payment for redelivery. All redelivery arrangements are free and handled through royalmail.com or the Royal Mail app. Hang up and arrange redelivery directly through official channels.

transcript.text: Hi, is that Grandma? It's me, Jamie. I'm in a bit of trouble — I've had a car accident abroad and I've been arrested. I'm okay but I need bail money urgently.
Please don't tell Mum and Dad, they'll be so worried. I need you to send £2,000 via Western Union today. My lawyer will give you the details.
Please hurry — I don't have much time to call.

cues: Unexpected emergency call from a family member is a known grandparent scam
Request to keep it secret from other family members prevents verification
Western Union transfers cannot be reversed once sent
Call back the family member on their known number to verify before doing anything
explanation: This is a grandparent scam targeting elderly people. The caller impersonates a grandchild in trouble to extract money. Always hang up and call the family member directly on their known number before taking any action. Never send money via Western Union based on an unsolicited call.

transcript.text: Good morning. This is the National Crime Agency. We have been monitoring suspicious financial transactions linked to your bank account as part of an ongoing investigation into money laundering.
Your account has been flagged and we need you to withdraw your savings in cash and transfer them to a secure government holding account using the details I will provide.
Do not speak to your bank about this as it may compromise the investigation. You have 90 minutes to comply before we freeze your assets.

cues: The NCA never contacts members of the public by phone to request cash withdrawals
No government agency asks you to withdraw cash and transfer it to a holding account
Instruction not to contact your bank is the biggest red flag possible
90-minute deadline is designed to create extreme panic and prevent rational thought
explanation: This is a sophisticated impersonation scam using the National Crime Agency name. No law enforcement agency ever asks you to withdraw cash or transfer money as part of an investigation. This is always a scam. Hang up immediately and call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040.

transcript.text: Hi, this is Dave from the IT support desk. We've had a report that your account credentials may have been compromised in a recent data breach.
I just need to verify your identity before I can lock down your account. Can you confirm your current username and password for me?
This will only take a moment and I can make sure your account is secured before any data is accessed.

cues: IT support never asks for your password — ever
Internal extension numbers can be spoofed
The caller contacted you — you cannot verify who they are
The right action is to hang up and call IT support back on the official number
A real IT team can reset your account without knowing your current password
explanation: This is a vishing attack impersonating internal IT support. No legitimate IT team ever needs your password — they have tools to reset or secure accounts without it. Hang up and call your IT helpdesk back using the official number from your company's intranet or directory.
